newsitem.title: USA: U.S. urges Cambodian factions to halt violence.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urges Cambodian factions to halt violence.

text.p: The United States on Sunday called on Cambodia's feuding factions to refrain from violence after sporadic fighting in the capital city of Phnom Penh prompted a group of 60 expatriates to flee the country.

No decision has been made on whether to evacuate the estimated 1,200 American citizens in Cambodia, including embassy personnel and their dependents, amid growing tension between troops loyal to the country's rival premiers, a State Department official said.

"The United States government calls on all parties to refrain from using violence, to resolve any differences through peaceful means and to abide by the terms of the Paris accords," the official said.
A peace accord was signed in Paris on Oct. 23, 1991, by four warring Cambodian factions and 18 countries setting out a plan for the transition to democracy.
"It is imperative that all parties contribute to conditions which will allow the elections scheduled for 1998 to take place," the U.S. official said.

The State Department warned all U.S. citizens against travel to Cambodia due to the political unrest and urged Americans already in the country to stay home day and night until the situation stabilises.
Any Americans who felt unsafe in their homes should go to the Sofitel Cambodiana Hotel in Phnom Penh, the department said in a travel warning issued on Sunday.

The U.S. Embassy in Phnom Penh reported that fighting in the capital subsided after a day of skirmishes in several locations and the imposition of a curfew from 8 p.m. until 6 a.m. There were also unconfirmed reports of fighting in some Cambodian provinces, the official said.
All Americans in the country were reported safe.
"The embassy is operating and continues to monitor the situation and to work to assure the welfare of American citizens," the official said.

With Phnom Penh airport closed, a group of 60 expatriates, including 18 Americans, fled Battambang in northwestern Cambodia into eastern Thailand on Sunday, according to Col. David Mead, the Australian defence attache who led them out.
U.S. Ambassador Kenneth Quinn has been in contact with both parties, including First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, who is out of the country, the official said.

The forces of FUNCINPEC, the royalist party headed by Ranariddh, control most of the area near the Thai border. His co-premier, Hun Sen, has tightened his grip on power in Phnom Penh where his forces outnumber Ranariddh's.
